additional_notes: Attached to a noun ending in a consonant (책이요, 당신이요). After a vowel, you usually just say “요” (커피요). Common in echo questions when you didn’t hear/are checking: “촬영이요?” ≈ “Filming?” In full sentences, this often corresponds to “이에요/예요” (e.g., 학생이에요).
native_language_example: A reservation? It’s for two tomorrow.

additional_notes: A casual command telling someone to release or stop holding something (or stop grabbing you). 놔 is the spoken contraction of 놓아 (from 놓다, “to let go/put down”). Can sound rude or aggressive depending on tone; use 제발 (“please”) to soften it (제발 이거 놔).
native_language_example: That hurts! Let go!

additional_notes: A casual way to get someone’s attention and show them something you’re holding or pointing to. Often said by itself (이거 봐!) or followed by a comment/question like 어때? (How is it?) or 예쁘지? (Isn’t it pretty?). You can repeat it for emphasis: 이거 봐, 이거!
native_language_example: Look at this—I made it myself.

meaning: “How about this?” / “What do you think of this?”
additional_notes: Used to suggest an idea or option and ask for the other person’s opinion. Very common in conversation when proposing something (“Then how about this?” = 그럼 이건 어때?). 이건 is a shortened form of 이것은 (“as for this”). Often said with a rising intonation as a question.
target_language_example: 시간이 없으면 내일 만나는 건 어때? 그럼 이건 어때?
native_language_example: If you don’t have time, how about meeting tomorrow? Then how about this?

meaning: “This, please” / “Look at this.” (used to get attention or ask for help with something).
additional_notes: Literally “this” + 좀 (“a bit”), but in everyday speech it’s often just a softener when asking someone to do something (like “please/just”). Common in requests: 이것 좀 봐 (Look at this), 이것 좀 들어봐/들어볼래? (Listen to this), 이것 좀 들어줘 (Hold this for me). On its own (이것 좀!) it can mean “Hey, look at this!” or “Excuse me—this!” depending on context and tone.
native_language_example: Wait a second—can you look at this for me?

meaning: “What is all this?” / “What is this all about?”
additional_notes: Literally “this + all,” used in questions to express surprise, confusion, or annoyance about a situation. Often followed by 뭐예요/뭡니까 (“what is it?”) or 무슨 일이죠 (“what’s going on?”).
native_language_example: What on earth is all this supposed to mean?

meaning: "What is this?" / "What’s going on?" (often expressing surprise or annoyance).
additional_notes: Very common informal spoken phrase. Literally "this (이게) + what (뭐) + is (야)". Depending on tone, it can be a neutral question (이게 뭐야?) or an exclamation of shock/irritation (이게 뭐야!). For a more polite version, use "이게 뭐예요?" or "이게 뭔가요?".
target_language_example: 어? 이게 뭐야? 내 지갑이 없어.
native_language_example: Huh? What’s going on? My wallet is gone.

meaning: "How is this…?" / "How could this…?" (often expressing disbelief).
additional_notes: Starts a question about a surprising or hard-to-believe situation. Common patterns: "이게 어떻게 + N(이/가) …?" (How is this N…?) and "이게 어떻게 된 거야?" (What happened?/How did this happen?). Often sounds like the speaker is shocked, upset, or incredulous rather than calmly asking for information.
native_language_example: How did this end up coming all the way here?

meaning: (Why are you) acting like this? / (Why are you) doing this?
additional_notes: Usually used with 왜 (“why”) to question someone’s behavior, often sounding annoyed, upset, or confused. It’s the spoken, casual style of 이러다 (“to act/be like this”) + -는 거야 (explaining/insisting tone). Can refer to someone’s words, attitude, or actions in the moment.
target_language_example: 갑자기 소리 지르지 마. 왜 이러는 거야?
native_language_example: Don’t suddenly yell. Why are you acting like this?

meaning: “this kind of thing” (as the object of the verb).
additional_notes: Spoken contraction of 이런 것(을): 이런 (“like this/this kind of”) + 것 (“thing”) + 을/를 (object marker). Used when reacting to or referring to something of this type, often with surprise or criticism (e.g., ‘How do you know this stuff?’ ‘Why sing this kind of thing?’).
native_language_example: Where did you learn this kind of thing?

additional_notes: A casual way to ask someone’s name, often to a friend or someone younger. Literally “(your) name is what?”. You’ll also hear/see: “너 이름이 뭐니?”, “네 이름이 뭐니?” (same meaning), or the more polite “이름이 뭐예요?/이름이 뭐야?”. Using “야,” before it can sound more abrupt (like “Hey,”).
native_language_example: We’re meeting for the first time—what’s your name?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s name or the name of something (a hotel, club, etc.). Very casual speech; with strangers, use the polite form “이름이 뭐예요?” or “성함이 어떻게 되세요?” for extra politeness. Often said as “(너/네) 이름이 뭐야?” (your name) or “(이거/그거) 이름이 뭐야?” (what is this called?).
native_language_example: What’s that store’s name?

additional_notes: A polite way to ask someone’s name, or the name of a person/animal mentioned in context. You can specify whose name by adding a noun before it (e.g., 개/남편/환자 이름이 뭐죠?). Literally “(The) name is what?” and uses the polite ending -죠 (softer than direct -예요/-입니까 in many situations).
native_language_example: Excuse me, what’s your name?

meaning: “What’s the name?” / “What was it called again?”
additional_notes: A casual way to ask for the name of a person, animal, place, or thing. Literally “(the) name + subject marker 이 + 뭐지 (what is it?)”. Often used when you’re trying to remember a name. More polite: 이름이 뭐예요?/이름이 뭐죠?
native_language_example: What’s that actor’s name again?

additional_notes: A casual command telling someone to come toward the speaker (“come this way/over here”). Often used when calling someone closer (kids, friends, pets). Softer/polite alternatives: 이리 오세요 (“Please come here”), 여기로 와/와 줘 (“Come here / come here for me”).
target_language_example: 잠깐만, 이리 와. 이거 좀 봐.
native_language_example: Wait a second—come here. Look at this.

additional_notes: An informal command meaning “give it to me (here).” Often said strongly or urgently, like when grabbing something away. You can add the object: "(그거) 이리 줘" (“Give me that.”). To sound a bit softer, say "이리 줘 봐" (“Let me see / give it to me for a second”) or add "좀" ("이리 줘 좀").
native_language_example: I’ll take a look at it. Give it here.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop or to suggest ending something. Often followed by a verb (e.g., 이제 그만 가자/갈까 “shall we go now?”) or used alone as a firm “That’s enough.” Can sound strong depending on tone; you can soften it with polite endings (e.g., 이제 그만하세요).
native_language_example: Let’s stop talking about it now.

meaning: “So what do we do now?” / “What happens now?”
additional_notes: Used to ask what the next step is from this point (“now”), often when you’re unsure, stuck, or waiting for instructions. It can be followed by verbs like 하다 (“do”) or 되다 (“become/happen”): 이제 어떻게 할 거야? (What will you do now?), 이제 어떻게 되는 거야? (What’s going to happen now?). Politeness changes with the ending: 해요/하죠 (polite), 해? (casual), 합니까? (formal).
native_language_example: A problem came up—so what do we do now?

additional_notes: Very common spoken, casual expression. Literally means “understanding doesn’t work/doesn’t happen,” but it’s used like “I don’t get it.” Often said alone, or followed by questions like 왜? (why?) or 뭐야? (what is it?). With rising intonation (이해가 안 돼?) it can mean “You don’t understand?” or “You don’t get it?” depending on context. Politer alternatives: 이해가 안 돼요, 이해가 안 됩니다.
target_language_example: 미안한데, 그 규칙은 아직 이해가 안 돼.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I still don’t understand that rule.

additional_notes: Casual/informal past-tense question used when you sense something happened (often something bad or unusual). Commonly appears as 무슨 일 있었어? or 뭔 일 있었어? (= shortened 무슨). Polite version: 일 있었어요? / 무슨 일 있었어요?
target_language_example: 얼굴이 안 좋아 보이는데, 무슨 일 있었어?
native_language_example: You don’t look well—did something happen?

additional_notes: A harsh command telling someone to stop talking. Literally means “close your mouth.” Commonly used in fights/insults and can be aggressive or threatening. Avoid in polite situations; softer alternatives include "조용히 해" (be quiet) or "잠깐만" (wait a second).
native_language_example: You’re being noisy. Shut up.

meaning: “Is there…?” / “Do you have…?” (casual question form of 있다).
additional_notes: From 있다 (“to exist; to have”) + -나 (casual question ending). Used to ask whether something exists/is available or whether someone has something: 커피는 있나? (“Do you have coffee?”). With a noun + 있나, it can sound blunt or even rude depending on tone/context (e.g., 귀도 있나? can imply “Are you even listening?”).
native_language_example: Do you have time now?

meaning: “(am/is/are) …-ing, right?” / “How/why am I (are you) …-ing?” (expressing confusion or realization).
additional_notes: Used most often as the ending **-고 있는 거지?** (from **-고 있다** “to be doing” + **것이지** → **거지**, casual). It adds a self-questioning/confirming tone: you’re trying to figure out what’s happening or why. Common in rhetorical questions like **내가 지금 뭐 하고 있는 거지?** “What am I even doing right now?”
target_language_example: 우리가 지금 뭘 기다리고 있는 거지?
native_language_example: What are we even waiting for right now?

meaning: “Is it that …?” / “Are you …?” (question form, often “Are you …-ing?” or “Do you have …?”).
additional_notes: Spoken contraction of **있는 것인가**. Commonly used in questions to ask for confirmation or to express surprise about what’s happening. Often follows **-고 있다** to mean “be -ing” (e.g., *싸우고 있는 건가?* “Are (they) fighting?”), or follows a noun/object to ask if someone has something (e.g., *뭘 가지고 있는 건가?* “What do you have?”).
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

additional_notes: From 있다 (“to exist / to be located”) + 거야 (casual explanatory ending, like “you know / it is that…”). Common in questions to ask where something/someone is or what situation exists: 어디에 있는 거야? (“Where is it/are you?”), 무슨 일이 있는 거야? (“What’s going on?”). It can also be used as a firm instruction meaning “stay put / just stay there” (often said to kids/pets): 얌전히 있는 거야 (“Stay still/behave and stay there.”).
native_language_example: Where are you right now?

meaning: “will be / will stay / there will be” (casual).
additional_notes: Future form of 있다 (“to be; to exist; to stay”). Used for (1) someone being/staying somewhere (같이 있을 거야, 보스턴에 있을 거야, 거기 있을 거야) and (2) something existing/being available (방법이 있을 거야 = “There will be a way.”). This is the casual ending; the polite version is 있을 거예요.
native_language_example: I’ll be at home tomorrow too.

additional_notes: Used to urge someone to do something right away. 자 is an attention-getting “okay/now/come on,” and 어서 means “quickly; hurry.” Common in casual speech and commands (often followed by a verb: 자, 어서 가! “Come on, go!”).
native_language_example: Come on, hurry up and come in!

additional_notes: Used in movie/TV credits after a person’s name to list their roles. 작가 means “writer” (screenwriter), and 제작 is short for “producer/production” (often effectively “producer” in credits). The comma just separates two roles: “writer, producer.”
native_language_example: Bong Joon-ho — writer, producer.

additional_notes: A casual goodbye said to someone who is leaving (the speaker is staying). Literally 'go well' (잘 = well, 가 = go). Often used with names or terms like 친구야. If you’re being polite to an older person/customer, use '안녕히 가세요' instead.
native_language_example: I’m going to go first. Bye, you too!

additional_notes: An imperative using the verb 들어요/듣다 (“to listen”). Often used to get someone’s attention before important instructions, advice, or a warning. Commonly said firmly (and can sound scolding depending on tone). You can also say it longer as “잘 들어(요)” or “내 말 잘 들어.”
target_language_example: 자, 다들 잘 들어. 지금부터 규칙을 설명할게.
native_language_example: Alright, everyone listen carefully. I’m going to explain the rules now.

additional_notes: Casual/plain style (…-겠어) often used to express uncertainty or not knowing something. Literally means “(I) don’t know well,” so it can soften “I don’t know” into “I’m not sure.” You can use it alone as a full answer.
native_language_example: I’m not sure if that movie is fun.

meaning: 'Be well / Take care' (also: 'Are you doing well?').
additional_notes: Casual phrase used (1) as a question meaning “Are you doing well?” or “Is (someone) doing okay?” (e.g., 파코는 잘 있어?), and (2) as a goodbye meaning “Take care / Bye” (잘 있어!). More polite: 잘 있어요. Similar idea: 잘 지내? (“How have you been?”).
native_language_example: I’m going to go first. Take care!

meaning: "Have you been well?" / "How have you been?" (casual).
additional_notes: A common casual greeting when you haven’t seen someone for a while. Literally “(you) were doing well,” from 잘 (well) + 있다 (to be/do) in past tense (있었어). Often used as a question: “잘 있었어?” For polite speech, use “잘 있었어요?” or to someone senior “잘 지내셨어요?” / “잘 계셨어요?”
native_language_example: Long time no see! How have you been?

additional_notes: From the verb 잘 지내다 (“to be doing well / to get along well”). In conversation it’s often used as a friendly check-in, usually as a question: 잘 지내? / 잘 지내요? You can also use it as a casual statement meaning “I’m doing well”: 나 잘 지내.
native_language_example: Long time no see! How have you been these days?

meaning: “Have you been well?” / “How have you been?”
additional_notes: A casual greeting used when meeting someone after some time. The ending -나 is an old-fashioned/masculine-sounding informal question style (often heard between men, in movies/dramas, or from an older person to someone younger). In everyday conversation, many people instead say 잘 지냈어? (to friends) or 잘 지내셨어요? (polite).
native_language_example: Long time no see. How have you been?

additional_notes: From 잡다 (to grab/hold) + -고 있다 (to be doing). Often used as a command in casual speech: “잡고 있어!” = “Hold on to it!” You can add what you’re holding with 을/를 (e.g., 손을 잡고 있어 = hold my hand). In a statement, the subject can be included: 내가 잡고 있어 = I’m holding it.
target_language_example: 가방 떨어질 것 같아. 내가 잡고 있어.
native_language_example: The bag might fall. I’m holding it.

additional_notes: 저 means “that (over there),” used for someone far from the speaker (often also far from the listener). It commonly points to a third person in the distance, and contrasts with 이 사람 (“this person” near me) and 그 사람 (“that person” near you / the person we mentioned). Can also be said alone as an exclamation to point someone out (저 사람!).
native_language_example: Who is that person?

additional_notes: 저 = “that (over there, away from both speaker and listener)”, 사람 = “person”, -은 = topic marker (“as for…”). Used to start a sentence about a specific person you’re pointing out (often with 누구야? “who is (that)?” or with a description like 선생님이에요/입니다 “(they) are a teacher”). In polite speech, the rest of the sentence changes (이에요/입니다), but 저 사람은 stays the same.
native_language_example: That person over there is an employee at our company.

additional_notes: A pointing phrase: 저 = “that (over there, away from both speaker and listener)” + 여자 = “woman.” Used to refer to a specific woman at some distance (“that woman over there”). Often followed by particles like 저 여자가… (“that woman [subject]…”) or 저 여자를… (“that woman [object]…”). Depending on tone/context, calling someone “저 여자” instead of “저 분/저분” (more polite) can sound blunt or disrespectful.
native_language_example: Who is that woman (over there)?

additional_notes: 저 = “that (over there)” (far from both speaker and listener). 여자 = “woman.” -는 marks the topic, often setting up a comment or question about her. Common in questions like “저 여자는 누구예요?” (“Who is that woman?”).
native_language_example: That woman is my teacher.

additional_notes: Used to ask what a thing is when it’s not close to the speaker/listener (저 = “that over there”). Very common as a reaction (surprise, curiosity, confusion) and can be said alone. More polite: 저게 뭐예요? / 저건 뭐예요?
native_language_example: What’s that? I’ve never seen it before.

additional_notes: A casual imperative used to draw someone’s attention to something you see (often while pointing). 저기 means “over there,” and 봐 is the casual form of 보다 (“to see/look”). More polite alternatives: 저기 보세요 / 저기 봐요.
native_language_example: Look over there! There’s a rainbow in the sky.

additional_notes: An imperative meaning “go over there and leave me alone.” Often used sharply/angrily (similar to “Go away!” or “Get lost!”). Commonly said alone as a command; can be intensified with words like “썩” (as in “썩 꺼져!” = “Get out of here!”). Not polite—avoid in formal situations.
native_language_example: I’m busy right now, so go away.

additional_notes: Used after a verb to talk about past experience: V-(으)ㄴ/ㄹ 적 있어요/있어? (e.g., 간 적 있어요? 해본 적 있어요?). Often with 한번이라도 (“even once/ever”). In casual speech you may hear just “적 있어(요)” with the verb understood from context.
native_language_example: Have you ever tried Korean food?

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the form -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다/없다 to talk about whether someone has had the experience of doing something. In questions, 적이 있나요? means “Have you ever done it?” Example patterns: 가본 적이 있나요? (Have you ever been?), 먹어본 적이 있나요? (Have you ever tried eating it?).
native_language_example: Have you ever tried Korean food?

meaning: "not (do) a phone call" / "don’t answer/call" (with 안 to negate).
additional_notes: 전화 means “a phone call,” and 안 is a common negation placed before a verb. This is usually used as part of a longer phrase like 전화 안 받았어? (You didn’t answer?), 전화 안 했어 (I didn’t call), 전화 안 와 (No call came / They didn’t call). It often appears in casual speech where particles are omitted.
target_language_example: 미안, 어제는 너무 바빠서 전화 안 했어.
native_language_example: Sorry, I was so busy yesterday that I didn’t call.

additional_notes: 전화 means “phone call/phone,” and 좀 is often added to make a request sound softer or less demanding (similar to “just” or “please”). What it means depends on the verb that follows: 전화 좀 해(줘) = “(Please) call (me/him),” 전화 좀 받아 = “(Please) pick up the phone.” Common in casual speech; you can make it more polite with 전화 좀 해 주세요 / 전화 좀 받아 주세요.
target_language_example: 시간 되면 나한테 전화 좀 해 줘.
native_language_example: If you have time, please call me.

meaning: “absolutely can’t / never can” (strongly saying something is impossible).
additional_notes: 절대 means “absolutely/never,” and 못 is used before a verb to mean “can’t (do).” Together, 절대 못 + verb is a strong, emphatic refusal or statement of impossibility. Common in spoken Korean: 절대 못 해(요) “I absolutely can’t do it,” 절대 못 가(요) “I can’t possibly go.” You can add politeness: 절대 못 해요 / 절대 못 합니다.
target_language_example: 오늘은 너무 바빠서 절대 못 가.
native_language_example: I’m so busy today that I absolutely can’t go.

additional_notes: 정말 adds emphasis (“really”). 미안해 is an informal/casual way to apologize, used to friends, family, or someone younger. For a polite version, use 정말 미안해요 or 정말 죄송해요.
native_language_example: I’m really sorry I’m late.

meaning: “Snap out of it,” “Get a grip,” or “Pay attention.”
additional_notes: An informal command (반말) from 정신 차리다 (“to pull yourself together/come to your senses”). Used when someone is distracted, acting irresponsibly, shocked, or not thinking clearly. It can sound sharp or scolding, so use with close friends/younger people; for a more polite version say 정신 차리세요.
target_language_example: 지금 장난할 때 아니야. 정신 차려.
native_language_example: This isn’t the time to joke around. Get a grip.

additional_notes: A common way to start a question about your own action. It’s a shortened form of "제가 무엇을" (I + what + object particle). "뭘" is the contraction of "무엇을" and is very common in speech. It’s often followed by a verb like 도와드리다 (help), 하다 (do), 말하다 (say), etc.
native_language_example: What should I do?

additional_notes: A repeated form of 제발 (“please”) used to strongly beg someone to stop, help, or agree. It sounds urgent and emotional (sometimes close to “for God’s sake”). You’ll often hear it shouted or said with pauses, and it can be followed by an imperative like 하지 마세요 (“don’t do it”).
native_language_example: Please, please help me.

additional_notes: Imperative form of 하다 (“to do”) with the adverb 조용히 (“quietly”). Used to tell someone to stop talking or making noise. 조용히 해요 is a softer polite version; 조용히 해 주세요 is more polite (“Please be quiet”); 조용히 해! can sound strong/commanding depending on tone and context. Often followed by a name or insult for emphasis (e.g., 조용히 해, 윌버! / 조용히 해, 이 녀석아!).
native_language_example: Guys, the movie has started. Be quiet.

additional_notes: Casual (banmal) command using 들어 (imperative of 듣다, “to listen”). 좀 literally means “a bit,” but here it softens the command to sound more like “please” or “just.” Often used with 내 말/내 얘기 (“my words/story”): 내 말 좀 들어 = “Listen to me.” If you add 줘 (들어 줘), it can also mean “Please do me a favor” in some contexts.
native_language_example: Wait a second—listen to me.

meaning: 'Look!' / 'Look at that!' (used to draw attention, often with surprise or criticism).
additional_notes: From 보다 (to see/look) + 좀 (“a bit”), but it’s usually not about “a bit”—it softens the command or adds an expressive tone. Common patterns: (1) "저기 좀 봐!" = “Look over there!” (2) "N(이/가) ~하는 것 좀 봐!" = “Look at (how) N is doing that!” often showing amazement, disbelief, annoyance, or scolding depending on tone.
target_language_example: 와, 하늘 좀 봐! 노을이 진짜 예쁘다.
native_language_example: Wow, look at the sky! The sunset is really pretty.

meaning: "How is it/are you?" (checking how someone/something is doing).
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s condition or situation: "몸은 좀 어때?" = “How are you feeling?” The word 좀 (“a bit”) softens the question and makes it sound less direct, like “How about…?” Without 요 (좀 어때?) it’s casual; with 요 (좀 어때요?) it’s more polite.
native_language_example: How have you been feeling lately?

meaning: How is it?/How are you feeling? (checking someone’s condition).
additional_notes:
Used to ask about someone’s state or situation (health, mood, how something is going). 
- With a topic: "몸은 좀 어때요?" = “How’s your body/How are you feeling?” 
- "좀" literally means “a bit,” but here it softens the question to sound gentler/less direct (like “How are you doing these days?”). 
Polite style (-어요).
native_language_example: How’s your cold—are you feeling any better?

meaning: “Want some?” / “Shall I give you some?” (offering something).
additional_notes: Used when offering something to someone in a casual, friendly way. Often the thing being offered comes right before it (e.g., 물 좀 줄까? “Want some water?”), and it can also be omitted if it’s clear from context (just 좀 줄까?). Form: 좀 (“a bit/just”) + 주다 (“to give”) + -(으)ㄹ까 (“shall I?/want me to?”). More casual than 드릴까요?
native_language_example: Are you hungry? Want some snacks?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to hand you something. Attach it to what you want: "Noun + 좀 줄래?" The word "좀" softens the request (like "just" / "a bit"), and "줄래" is casual/informal, so use it with friends, family, or someone younger. Politer alternatives: "좀 주세요" or "좀 주실래요?"
native_language_example: Could you give me a glass of water?

meaning: “(Please) do it.” / “Do it a bit.” (a softened command/request).
additional_notes: Used after a verb (often 하다) to make a request or command sound less blunt. In real life it can still sound impatient or like nagging depending on tone, especially in sentences like “조용히 좀 해!” (“Be quiet, please!”). This is informal speech (해체), used with friends, family, or someone younger.
native_language_example: Please decide quickly.

additional_notes: An informal imperative using 해 보다 (“to try doing”). The particle 좀 literally means “a bit,” but here it softens the command into a request—though in contexts like 대답 좀 해봐! it can still sound impatient (“Come on, answer”). Often used after a noun/verb phrase: 말 좀 해봐 (Say something), 생각 좀 해봐 (Think about it), 어떻게 좀 해봐 (Do something about it).
target_language_example: 나 좀 도와줘. 이거 한번 해봐.
native_language_example: Help me. Try doing this once.

additional_notes: A common morning greeting. Often used on its own (좋은 아침!) or followed by a name or a follow-up question (좋은 아침, 잘 잤어?). It’s neutral/polite in tone; for a more formal greeting you can also say 안녕하세요 in the morning.
native_language_example: Good morning—you came early today!

meaning: “a good day” (used in greetings like “Have a good day!”).
additional_notes: Most often used in polite set phrases: 좋은 하루 되세요! (“Have a good day!”) or 좋은 하루 보내세요 (“Spend/Have a good day”). 되세요 sounds like “be (that way),” while 보내세요 literally means “spend,” but both function as a friendly farewell to customers, strangers, or anyone you want to be polite to.
native_language_example: Have a good day today too!

additional_notes: Future form of 죽다 (to die): 죽- + -(으)ㄹ 거야. Used to predict something (“He’ll probably die soon”) or as a dramatic exclamation (“We’re all going to die!”). Often implies strong emotion or urgency; a polite version is 죽을 거예요.
native_language_example: At this rate, we’re all going to die!

additional_notes: Casual/informal future form: 죽이다 (to kill) + -(으)ㄹ 거야 (going to / will). It’s a very strong phrase and can sound like a real threat. In casual speech it can also be used as an exaggeration (like “I’m gonna kill you!” meaning “I’m so mad!”), but use with caution. More polite: 죽일 거예요. To say “I’m going to die” (not kill someone), use 죽을 거야 (different verb form).
native_language_example: If you lie, I’m seriously going to kill you.

additional_notes: A strong, emotional command used to beg someone not to die. Literally “don’t die,” formed from 죽다 (to die) + -지 마 (don’t). Often used with 제발 (“please”) or names/vocatives (e.g., 죽지 마, 민수야).
target_language_example: 제발 죽지 마, 나 아직 할 말이 있어.
native_language_example: Please don’t die—I still have something to say.

additional_notes: Comes from 주다 (to give) + -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다 (can/can’t). Commonly used as 줄 수 있어요/있나요? (can you give…?) or 줄 수 없어요 (can’t give…). You’ll also see 줄 수는… with 는 to add contrast or emphasis (e.g., “I can’t give it to you, though”).
native_language_example: I can't give you that right now.

additional_notes: Comes from 주다 (to give) + -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다 (can/can’t). Commonly used as 줄 수 있어요/있나요? (can you give…?) or 줄 수 없어요 (can’t give…). You’ll also see 줄 수는… with 는 to add contrast or emphasis (e.g., “I can’t give it to you, though”).
native_language_example: I can't give you that right now.

additional_notes:
Used in the grammar pattern -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다 after a verb.

1) Assumption/belief about a fact: “(I) think/suppose that…” Often used in questions to challenge someone’s assumption: “내가 ~인 줄 알아?” = “Do you think I’m ~?”

2) Ability/skill: “know how to…” Commonly with 하다: “할 줄 알아” = “know how to do it.”

Past: -(으)ㄴ 줄 알아 = “thought that…”. Negative: -(으)ㄹ 줄 모르다 = “don’t know how to / didn’t know that…”.
native_language_example: I know how to drive.

additional_notes: Used in the pattern -(으)ㄹ 줄 알아요 after a verb to say you know how to do something (a skill/ability): 운전할 줄 알아요? “Do you know how to drive?” It can also mean “to know/realize” a fact after an action or description, often in questions like ~인 줄 알아요? or ~하는 줄 알아요? (“Do you know/realize that…?” / “Do you know what … is like?”). Polite present form; past is 줄 알았어요 (“I thought/knew…”), negative is 줄 몰라요 (“I don’t know how to / I didn’t know that…”).
native_language_example: I know how to greet someone in Korean.

additional_notes:
Used after a clause to say you believed something to be true, or expected something to happen. Common patterns: 
• -(으)ㄹ 줄 알았다 = thought/expected someone would do something (future/action): 네가 올 줄 알았다. (“I thought you’d come.”)
• -은/는 줄 알았다 = thought something was the case (state/past): 그가 화난 줄 알았다. (“I thought he was angry.”)
Often said as an exclamation: 그럴 줄 알았다! (“I knew it!”).
target_language_example: 비가 올 줄 알았는데 안 왔어요.
native_language_example: I thought it would rain, but it didn’t.

additional_notes: Casual/polite-level informal (반말) past form of -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다. It’s used to say you believed something would happen or was true (often as a prediction or assumption), and it can imply you might have been wrong once the real situation is known. Pattern: [Verb-(으)ㄹ 줄 알았어]. Note: -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다 can also mean "to know how to (do something)" (ability), but in many contexts like "그럴 줄 알았어" it means "I knew/figured it would be like that."
native_language_example: I thought you would come too.

additional_notes: Used with a verb/adjective + -(으)ㄴ/는 지 to ask about the time elapsed since something happened or a state began. Very often followed by 얼마나 됐어/됐어요? (“has it been?”). Examples: 만난 지 얼마나 됐어? (How long has it been since we met? / since you met them?), 한국에 온 지 얼마나 됐어요? (How long have you been in Korea?).
target_language_example: 우리 마지막으로 만난 지 얼마나 됐지?
native_language_example: How long has it been since we last met?

meaning: "What (are you) doing now?" / "What are you doing? (right now)"
additional_notes: Often used before a verb, especially 하다: 지금 뭐 해(요)? = “What are you doing right now?” Depending on tone and situation, it can sound surprised, annoyed, or confrontational (“What do you think you’re doing?”). Polite: 지금 뭐 하세요?/하시는 거예요? Casual: 지금 뭐 해? / 지금 뭐 하는 거야? You can also use it to challenge a suggestion: 지금 뭐 하자는 거야? = “What are you trying to do (now)?”
target_language_example: 지금 뭐 하는 거예요? 여기서 이러면 안 돼요.
native_language_example: What are you doing right now? You can’t do that here.

additional_notes: A very common way to ask someone’s current location. It’s often followed by 있어/있어? (be), 가(요)? (go), or 있는지 알아? (do you know where someone is). The subject (you/he/she/we) is frequently omitted and understood from context: 지금 어디 있어? = “Where are you now?”
native_language_example: Where are you right now?

meaning: 'at home right now' / 'to home right now' (depends on the verb).
additional_notes: 지금 = 'now/right now' and 집에 = 'at home/to home' (location marker 에 can mean 'at' with 있다/없다, and 'to' with 가다/오다). So 지금 집에 is often used before verbs like 있어요/없어요 ('(am) at home / not at home') or 갈 수 있다 ('can go home now').
native_language_example: I'm at home right now.

additional_notes: 집 means “house/home,” and -에 marks a place you are at (location) or a place you go to (destination), depending on the verb. So 집에 있어요 = “(I’m) at home,” and 집에 가요/왔어요 = “go/come home.” You can also say 누구 집에 (“at/to whose house”) or 어머니 집에 (“to/at my mother’s house”).
native_language_example: Today I’m going to go home early.

meaning: (in 무슨/이런 짓을 하다) “to do (such) a thing” / “what are you doing?!” (often accusing).
additional_notes: Comes from 짓 (“act/deed”) + 하다 (“to do”). Very commonly used as 무슨 짓을 하는 거야? (“What are you doing?!”) or 왜 이런 짓을 해? (“Why are you doing this?!”). It often carries a negative, shocked, or scolding tone (you think the action is wrong or ridiculous). You’ll also see stronger versions like 미친 짓 (“crazy thing to do”).
target_language_example: 지금 여기서 무슨 짓을 하는 거야?
native_language_example: What are you doing here right now?!

additional_notes: 짓 means a “deed/act,” and in this pattern it usually implies something wrong, shocking, or suspicious. It’s commonly used in questions like 무슨/뭔 짓을 한 거야? (“What on earth did you do?”). The ending -거야 is casual/informal (often used with friends, family, or when confronting someone).
target_language_example: 너 어제 대체 무슨 짓을 한 거야?
native_language_example: What on earth did you do yesterday?

additional_notes: 찾다 (“to find/look for”) + -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 (“can/be able to”). It’s usually followed by 있어요/있어/있습니다 (e.g., 찾을 수 있어요 = “I can find it”). With 없다, it becomes “can’t find” (찾을 수 없어/없어요). Often used after an object marked with 을/를: 방법을 찾을 수 있어 (“can find a way”).
target_language_example: 이 주소를 인터넷에서 찾을 수 있어요.
native_language_example: You can find this address on the internet.

additional_notes: Informal spoken form of "필요 없다" (“to not need; to be unnecessary”). The subject and object are often omitted and understood from context: e.g., "그럴 필요 없어" = “No need to do that,” "거짓말 할 필요 없어" = “You don’t need to lie.” When said to a person ("너 필요 없어"), it can sound harsh: “I/We don’t need you.”
native_language_example: I don’t need this anymore.

additional_notes: 필요하다 (“to need”) + -는 (modifier) + 거 (short for 것, “thing”). Common in conversation (especially in stores) to ask if someone needs help or needs anything: 필요한 거 있어요? = “Do you need anything?” You can also say 필요한 거 없어요? (“You don’t need anything?”) or 필요한 거 있어요? (“Is there anything you need?”).
native_language_example: If you need anything, please let me know.

meaning: “Do you want to do (it)?” (asking someone what they want to do).
additional_notes: Combination of 하고 싶다 (“to want to do”) + 니? (casual question ending). Used with a verb in 해/하다 form (e.g., 뭐 하고 싶니? “What do you want to do?”). Casual/informal; use with friends, family, or kids. More polite alternatives: 하고 싶어요? / 하고 싶으세요?
native_language_example: What do you want to do this weekend?

meaning: 'want to (do)' / 'that you want to (do or say)'.
additional_notes: From the pattern -(으)고 싶다 (“to want to do”). 하고 싶은 is the noun-modifying form, used before a noun: 하고 싶은 말 (something you want to say), 하고 싶은 일 (something you want to do). It can refer to wanting to *do* an action, but it’s also commonly used with 말/얘기 to mean “something you want to say.” Standard spacing is 하고 싶은.
target_language_example: 지금 하고 싶은 말 있으면 해도 돼.
native_language_example: If you have something you want to say now, you can say it.

meaning: “(What) are you doing?” / “(What) are you talking about?” (ongoing action, often with surprise/annoyance).
additional_notes: Built from -고 있다 (to be doing, ongoing) + 거야 (casual/explanatory ending). Commonly used in questions like 뭐/뭘 하고 있는 거야? (“What are you doing?”), 무슨 얘기를 하고 있는 거야? (“What are you talking about?”), 여기서 뭐 하고 있는 거야? (“What are you doing here?”). With words like 도대체/대체 it sounds more frustrated or shocked (“What on earth…?”).
target_language_example: 지금 여기서 뭐 하고 있는 거야?
native_language_example: What are you doing here right now?

meaning: "(I’m/you’re/etc.) doing (it)"; "(I’m/you’re/etc.) in the middle of doing (it)".
additional_notes: From the verb ending -고 있다 (here shown as 하고 있어), used to describe an action in progress (present continuous). It attaches to a verb stem: 공부하고 있어요 = “I’m studying.” In questions like 뭐 하고 있어? / 지금 뭘 하고 있어? it means “What are you doing (right now)?” It can also be used alone to confirm/insist: 하고 있어! = “I am!” / “I’m doing it!” (informal; polite would be 하고 있어요/하고 있습니다).
target_language_example: 지금 뭐 하고 있어? 나 숙제하고 있어.
native_language_example: What are you doing right now? I’m doing my homework.

additional_notes: Polite conversational form of the ongoing-action pattern -고 있어요, attached to a verb stem (하다 → 하고 있어요). Used for actions happening now or around now: 뭐 하고 있어요? = “What are you doing?” In speech/writing, spacing may vary (뭐 하고 있어요 / 뭐하고 있어요) but the meaning is the same.
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

additional_notes: Used to count down and cue a group action (go, start, turn, lift, take a photo, etc.). Often followed by an action verb like 가자/갑시다 (“let’s go”), 시작하자 (“let’s start”), or 돌려 (“turn it”). You can also say it alone as a quick signal to begin.
native_language_example: Okay—one, two, three! Let’s start.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or mention an extra item/action: 하나 더 있어요 (“There’s one more.”), 하나 더 빌어 (“Make one more wish.”), 하나 더 던져 (“Throw one more.”). In conversation it can be a short question meaning “One more?” (confirming or offering). Often used when ordering too: (커피) 하나 더 주세요 (“One more (coffee), please.”).
target_language_example: 물 한 병 하나 더 주세요.
native_language_example: One more bottle of water, please.

meaning: "(are) you doing?" / "(are) you saying?" (often with surprise or anger).
additional_notes: Spoken casual ending (반말), from **하는 것이야** → **하는 거야**. Used after a verb to question or challenge what someone is doing/saying, often sounding accusatory: **뭐 하는 거야?** “What are you doing?” **무슨 소릴 하는 거야?** “What are you talking about?” Can also appear as **…하는 거야?** after other verbs (e.g., **왜 그러는 거야?** “Why are you doing that?”).
native_language_example: What are you doing here right now?

additional_notes: From 하다 (to do) + -는 것 (turns a verb into “the act of …ing”) + -이에요/예요 (to be). It’s commonly used to ask what someone is doing or to explain what you’re doing. The subject is often omitted and understood from context: e.g. (지금) 뭐 하는 거예요? = “What are you doing (now)?” With 무슨/뭐라고, it can sound like “What are you talking about?” depending on tone.
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

additional_notes: A casual spoken ending: 하다 + -(는) 것 + -이지(= -지). It’s used when the speaker is asking themselves or someone else what’s going on, often with confusion, doubt, or mild accusation (like “What do you think you’re doing?”). Common with question words: 뭐/무슨/왜 + … 하는 거지?
native_language_example: What are you doing right now?

additional_notes: Imperative negative command: 하다 (“to do”) + -지 마 (“don’t”). Used to tell someone not to do an action, often strongly in warnings/scolding. Commonly follows a noun + 하다 action (거짓말 하지 마 = “don’t lie”) or can stand alone as “Don’t!”; can also be used after another verb stem: 가지 마 (“don’t go”), 말하지 마 (“don’t say it”).
target_language_example: 지금 전화하지 마. 나 회의 중이야.
native_language_example: Don’t call right now. I’m in a meeting.

additional_notes: A polite negative command meaning “don’t do [that].” It’s made from 하다 (“to do”) + -지 마세요 (“please don’t…”). You can replace 하다 with other verbs: 가지 마세요 (Don’t go), 말하지 마세요 (Don’t speak). Stronger/more urgent in tone when paired with words like 제발 (“please/beg you”).
native_language_example: Please don’t take photos here.

meaning: “(I said) don’t do it” / “tell (someone) not to do it.”
additional_notes: From 하다 (“to do”) + -지 말다 (“don’t do”) + -라고 (quoting what you said/told someone). Used when repeating or stressing a warning/command: “I told you not to do it,” or shouted as “Don’t do it!” Often followed by 하다/말하다: 하지 말라고 해(요) (“Tell them not to do it”). Can sound harsh depending on tone; adding insults makes it very rude.
native_language_example: I told you not to go in there!

meaning: 'have to go to school' / 'must go to school' (used before 돼/해/합니다).
additional_notes: 학교에 = “to school” (학교 + 에). 가야 is 가다 (“to go”) + -아/어야, which expresses necessity (“have to/must”). It’s usually completed with something like 돼/돼요 (casual/polite), 해/해요 (casual/polite), or 합니다/됩니다 (formal): 학교에 가야 돼요 = “I have to go to school.”
native_language_example: I have to go to school today.

additional_notes: 대 is a counter mainly used for machines and vehicles (e.g., cars, computers, washing machines). It’s also commonly used for one cigarette (one stick), especially in casual speech: 담배 한 대. In contexts involving a washing machine, 한 대 can mean “one load / one cycle” (i.e., one run of the machine), depending on what’s understood from the situation.
native_language_example: I have one car.

additional_notes:
Use **한 마리** to count animals (cats, dogs, horses, cows, sheep, etc.). **한** = “one” before a counter, and **마리** is the counter. Adding **-가** makes it the subject of the sentence (“one animal *does/is* …”).

Pattern: **[animal] 한 마리가 + verb/adjective** (e.g., 앉아 있어요, 있어요, 보여요/안 보여요). If you want the object instead, you’ll often see **한 마리를**.
target_language_example: 강아지 한 마리가 문 앞에 서 있어요.
native_language_example: One puppy is standing in front of the door.

additional_notes: Uses the native Korean number 한 (from 하나, “one”) + the counter 명 for people. Common in phrases like 한 명 더 (one more person), 한 명도 없다 (not even one person), and with 있다/없다 to say how many people there are. Often interchangeable with 한 사람, but 명 is a more neutral/polite counting word.
target_language_example: 여기 한 명만 들어갈 수 있어요.
native_language_example: Only one person can go in here.

additional_notes: Literally “one time.” Very common with action verbs to suggest trying something: “V-(아/어) 보다” (해봐 = try it; 보여줘 봐 = show me/let me see). It can also emphasize that something happened zero times when used with negatives: “한 번도 …없다” = “not even once.” In suggestions/encouragement, “한 번 해보자” means “let’s give it a try.”
target_language_example: 시간 있으면 그 식당에 한 번 가 봐.
native_language_example: If you have time, try going to that restaurant (once).

additional_notes: Used with negative expressions like 안/못/없다 to emphasize that something has happened zero times. Literally “even one time,” so it commonly appears as 한 번도 안/못/없어(요).
target_language_example: 저는 한국에 한 번도 가 본 적이 없어요.
native_language_example: I've never been to Korea (not even once).

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens only a single time, or to make a strong request like “just this once.” Often appears with verbs (e.g., 한 번만 해 봐, 한 번만 말해 봐) and can sound pleading or insistent depending on tone.
native_language_example: Please let it slide just this once.

additional_notes: Counter phrase: 한 (one) + 잔 (counter for drinks served in a cup/glass, including alcohol). Often used when offering or suggesting a drink (커피 한 잔?, 술 한 잔 하다 = ‘have a drink’). You can add 더 to mean “one more” (한 잔 더).
target_language_example: 시간 있으면 커피 한 잔 할래요?
native_language_example: If you have time, want to have a cup of coffee?

meaning: "(you) did" / "did you do (it)?" (casual, often in questions).
additional_notes: Casual spoken form of **한 것이야** (past of **하다** + **것** + **이다**). Used to ask what someone did, how they did it, or what they were thinking: **뭘/뭐를 한 거야?** (What did you do?), **어떻게 한 거야?** (How did you do it?), **무슨 생각을 한 거야?** (What were you thinking?). Often sounds like demanding an explanation. Plain form **한 거야?** means “Did you do it?” / “Is that what you did?”
native_language_example: Wait, did you do this by yourself?

meaning: "(You/they) did/said (it), right?" (asking what happened or seeking confirmation)
additional_notes: Short for "한 거예요/한 거죠" = 하다 + -(으)ㄴ 것 (the thing that was done) + 이다. Used most often in questions like "뭐 한 거죠?" (What did you do?) or "뭐라고 한 거죠?" (What did you say?). It can sound like you’re pressing for an explanation, sometimes with surprise or suspicion, depending on tone/context.
native_language_example: What did you just say?

additional_notes: Spoken/casual shortening of **한 것이지** (often also understood as **했지** depending on context). It follows a past action (**한**) + “thing” (**거**) + ending **-지**, which adds a tone of explanation/confirmation (“you know / I mean / after all”). Common in rhetorical questions like **내가 무슨 짓을 한 거지?** (“What did I do?”) or **대체 어떻게 한 거지?** (“How on earth did [they] do it?”).
native_language_example: I did your share too (that’s what I did).

additional_notes: Formed from 하다 (to do) + -ㄹ/을 거야 (will/going to). Often used in casual speech and questions about someone’s plan or intention: “그래서 어떻게 할 거야?” = “So what are you going to do?” The subject is usually omitted and understood from context. In writing or polite speech, you’ll often see 할 거예요 / 할 겁니다 instead.
native_language_example: I’m definitely going to do it tomorrow.

meaning: “will do / am going to do” (polite future or intention).
additional_notes: Built from 하다 (“to do”) + -(ㄹ) 거예요, a very common way to talk about future plans or intentions in polite speech. Often used in questions to ask what someone will do (뭐 할 거예요?) or how they will handle something (어떻게 할 거예요?). Spacing is often written as 할 거예요 or 할거예요.
native_language_example: I’m going to study at home today.

meaning: (plain) “Are you going to do (it)?” / “What will you do?”
additional_notes: Contraction of 할 것인가. Used to ask about someone’s plan or what they intend to do next. It’s the plain (non-polite) question style, so it can sound blunt; in polite speech you’d often use 할 건가요? or 할 거예요? The object is often understood from context (e.g., 이제 뭘 할 건가? “What are you going to do now?”).
native_language_example: What are you going to do with that money?

meaning: “(someone) is going to do (it),” often with a “then/so…” nuance (casual).
additional_notes: A contracted form of 할 것인데 (sometimes 할 건데요 when more polite). Used a lot in questions like 누가 할 건데? (“Who’s going to do it, then?”) or 뭐 할 건데? (“What are you going to do (about it/with that), then?”). The -는데/-건데 ending can add a feeling of contrast, background, or “so/then…?” depending on context.
native_language_example: So what are you going to do now?

meaning: “something to say” (words you want/need to say).
additional_notes: Literally “words to say” (할 = “to do/say” + 말 = “words”). Commonly used in questions like 할 말 있어요? (“Do you have something to say?”) or 할 말 없어요? (“Nothing to say?”). You can add 또 (“more/again”) or 더 (“more”) to ask if someone has anything else to say: 또/더 할 말 있어요?
native_language_example: If you have something to say, say it now.

meaning: 'something to say' (as in 'I/you have something to say').
additional_notes: From 하다 (to do) + 말 (words) + -이 (subject marker). It’s used before 있다/없다 to ask or state whether someone has anything to say: 할 말이 있어요/없어요. In questions it can sound confrontational depending on tone: 할 말이 없냐? (“Got nothing to say?”). Often followed by 있어서 (because/if there is something to say): 할 말이 있어서 왔어요 (“I came because I had something to say”).
native_language_example: I have something to say.

meaning: 'can / be able to (do)' (used as -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다).
additional_notes: Used with 있다 or 없다 to express ability/possibility: 할 수 있다 = can do (it), 할 수 없다 = can’t do (it). The verb before 수 is in the -(으)ㄹ form: 하다→할 수, 먹다→먹을 수, 가다→갈 수. Often appears as a fixed chunk in phrases like 할 수 있어요/없어요 (“I can/can’t”).
native_language_example: I can’t help you today.

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to say you have the ability to do something. Often used with an action verb: e.g. 수영을 할 수 있습니다 (can swim). With languages, it means “can speak/do [a language]”: 한국어를 할 수 있습니다 (can speak Korean). The dictionary form is 할 수 있다; 입니다-style politeness makes it 할 수 있습니다.
native_language_example: I can drive.

meaning: “(You/I/etc.) can do it / be able to do it.”
additional_notes: From 하다 (“to do”) + -(으)ㄹ 수 있다/없다 (“can/can’t; be able/unable to”). 할 수 있어 is the informal present-tense style (often used with friends, kids, or in encouragement). Commonly used as a pep talk meaning “You can do it!”; more polite: 할 수 있어요. To specify the action, put a verb in the -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 form: 수영을 할 수 있어 (“can swim”), 한국어를 읽을 수 있어 (“can read Korean”).
target_language_example: 걱정 마, 우리 할 수 있어!
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we can do it!

additional_notes: Used to say you have the ability/possibility to do something. Often follows a verb in the -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 form (e.g., 만들 수 있어요 “I can make (it)”), or is used alone to encourage/reassure someone (“할 수 있어요!” = “You can do it!”). Polite speech level.
native_language_example: I can do it by myself.

meaning: “(I/you) have something to say / talk about …” (used before 있다/없다).
additional_notes: Usually appears as 할 얘기가 있어(요) “I have something to talk about” or 할 얘기가 없어(요) “I don’t have anything to say.” It’s often used to introduce a topic (sometimes serious) or to challenge someone: 할 얘기 없어? “Nothing to say?” The full phrase is 할 얘기 “something to talk about” + subject marker 가, so it typically needs a verb like 있다/없다 after it.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I have something to talk about.

meaning: “things to do” / “a task (that someone) should do” (often with 있다/없다/많다).
additional_notes: From 할 일 (“something to do”) + the subject marker 이/가. Common patterns: 할 일이 있어요/없어요 (“I have/don’t have anything to do”), 할 일이 많아요 (“I have a lot to do”), 할 일이 아니에요 (“It’s not (someone’s) job/it’s not their place to do it”). Often used to talk about duties or chores.
target_language_example: 지금 할 일이 많아서 나중에 전화할게요.
native_language_example: I have a lot to do right now, so I’ll call you later.

additional_notes: Usually appears in patterns like **-(으)ㄹ 줄 알다** (“to know how to; can”) and **-(으)ㄹ 줄 모르다** (“don’t know how to; can’t”). It’s commonly used for skills (languages, swimming, cooking) and can also mean “know how to do it (properly)” as in making a joke. Attach **-(으)ㄹ** to the verb stem: **하다 → 할 줄**, **먹다 → 먹을 줄**, **읽다 → 읽을 줄**.
native_language_example: I know how to drive.

meaning: know how to do (something); can do.
additional_notes: Pattern: verb stem + -(으)ㄹ 줄 알다. Used to say someone has the skill/ability to do something, or to ask if they can do it. Often appears as a question (할 줄 알아?) or in other speech levels: 할 줄 알아요 (polite), 할 줄 압니다 (formal). Not about knowing a fact, but knowing how to perform an action.
native_language_example: Do you know how to swim?

meaning: “Shall I do it for you?” / “Want me to do it (for you)?”
additional_notes: A casual way to offer to do something for someone. It’s the pattern -아/어 줄까? (“Shall I … for you?”), with 해 from 하다 (“to do”) and 주다 meaning doing it as a favor/for someone. Often used when offering help (e.g., 설명해 줄까? “Want me to explain?”).
native_language_example: Want me to make the reservation for you?

meaning: 'can pull it off' / 'be able to do it (successfully)'.
additional_notes: Usually used as the start of the pattern **해낼 수 있다/없다** (“can/can’t pull it off”). **해내다** means to accomplish something despite difficulty, so it often sounds encouraging or confident (similar to “You can do it!”).
native_language_example: I can do it even by myself.

meaning: “Is it okay if I do it?” / “Can I do it?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for permission. It comes from the verb 하다 (“to do”) + -(아/어)도 돼(요) (“it’s okay even if…” → “it’s okay to…”). Very common on its own (해도 돼?) or after a noun + 하나 (“one thing”): 부탁 하나 해도 돼? (“Can I ask a favor?”). Politer versions: 해도 돼요? / 해도 될까요?
native_language_example: Is it okay if I speak now? / Can I say it now?

meaning: “Is it okay if I do (it)?” / “Can I do (it)?” (asking permission).
additional_notes: Used after a verb stem to ask if something is allowed/okay. Common pattern: Verb + -아/어도 돼요? (e.g., 가도 돼요? “Can I go?”, 먹어도 돼요? “Can I eat?”). With 하다-verbs, it becomes 해도 돼요. A polite, everyday way to ask permission.
native_language_example: Can I sit here?

additional_notes: Spoken, casual form of 해야 돼/해야 합니다, used to say something is necessary or required. It comes from 하다 (to do) + -아/어야 하다 (must/should). Often used with a verb stem: 가야 해 (have to go), 먹어야 해 (have to eat). The subject is often omitted when obvious: 해야 해 = “(I/you) have to.”
native_language_example: I have to go to bed early today.

additional_notes: Comes from 하다 (“to do”) + -아/어야 하다 (“must/need to”). Attach -아/어야 해요 to a verb stem to say you have to do something: 가야 해요 (have to go), 먹어야 해요 (have to eat). Often implies obligation/necessity; can be softened with 것 같아요 (“I think I have to…”).
native_language_example: I have to leave now.
